name: Design a Search Relevance Pipeline
intent: Decide the order of product search results: understand the query, fetch a few thousand candidates cheaply, re-rank the best few hundred with a learned model inside the latency budget, and learn from clicks without fooling yourself.
codeTitle: turning position-biased clicks into a better order, and scoring it with NDCG
finalIntro: One shopper typing a query and getting an order that is learned, measured and kept honest.
prompt: Design the ranking of search results for a store with 100 million products and 50 million searches a day. Finding products that match is already solved by an inverted index. The job is the order of the first page: the most relevant and most likely to be bought should come first, new products should get a fair chance, and the whole search must answer in about 150 ms. You must be able to prove that a new ranking is better before everyone gets it.
functional: Fix spelling, expand synonyms and detect what the shopper means before matching
Retrieve candidates from the inverted index and score them cheaply with text and business signals
Re-rank the top few hundred candidates with a learned model
Log what was shown, at which position, and what was clicked or bought
Evaluate a new ranking offline on judged queries and online in an A/B test
Give new products a chance to be seen
nonFunctional: The whole search answers in about 150 ms at p99, with a hard stop for the re-ranker
Re-rank 200 to 500 candidates per search, not the whole catalogue
Features such as price, stock, recent sales and freshness are no more than minutes old
If the re-ranker or the feature store is slow or down, the search still returns the cheap ordering
Every ranking change is measured before it reaches all traffic and can be rolled back with a flag
Training data must not be distorted by the old ranking

firstAttempt.text: One SQL query: WHERE title LIKE '%words%' ORDER BY sales_last_30_days DESC LIMIT 10. Typos and synonyms are not handled, and the order is simply the best sellers among the matches.
limits: A leading wildcard scans the whole table, so it cannot meet 150 ms at 50 million searches a day
Best sellers always win, so a perfect match for the words can sit below a loosely related popular product
A typo or a synonym (sneakers, trainers) returns nothing at all
There is no way to tell whether a new order is better, so changes are made by opinion
New products have no sales, so they never get shown and never get sales

steps.title: Understand the query before matching it
steps.problem: Shoppers type 'runing shoos for wmen', 'sneakers' when the catalogue says 'trainers', or just 'apple'. Matching the raw words finds nothing, or the wrong thing, and the best ranking in the world cannot order products that were never retrieved.
steps.fix: A query understanding step runs first and has a budget of about 10 ms. It normalises the text, corrects spelling using the index's own vocabulary and the most frequent past queries, expands synonyms from a curated and mined dictionary, and classifies intent: which category the words most likely mean (shoes, not phones), whether it is a brand or a model number, and which attributes were named (size, colour). Its output is a structured query, with the original words kept and the rewrites given a lower weight. Frequent queries are cached whole, because a few hundred thousand distinct queries cover most of the traffic.
steps.tradeoff: A better recall and a precise intent come before anything else in the pipeline. A wrong rewrite hurts silently, for example 'apple' read as the fruit in an electronics store, so rewrites keep a lower weight than the original words, and are measured like any other change.

steps.title: Retrieve candidates and score them cheaply
steps.problem: Scoring 100 million products with a heavy model for each search is impossible. But the final order is only as good as the candidates it is chosen from, and the first stage must be both fast and not too crude.
steps.fix: Use the inverted index to find every product that matches the structured query, shard by shard, and score them with BM25 on title, brand and description fields, plus a few cheap business signals that are stored in the index: category match, in stock, a popularity prior, a freshness factor and a quality score. Each shard keeps its best 500 or so, and the coordinator merges them into the top 2,000, which is the candidate set. This stage should finish in about 40 ms. A recall check is part of the design: the products that sellers and shoppers eventually buy must be inside the candidate set for the later stages to rank them.
steps.tradeoff: The index does the heavy lifting with a score that costs microseconds per product. The price is that the first-stage score is crude, so a product that the re-ranker would have loved can be cut here, and candidate recall has to be measured, not assumed.

steps.title: Re-rank the top few hundred with a learned model
steps.problem: BM25 and a handful of hand-set weights do not know that shoppers who type 'laptop' want a recent model with good reviews, or that the price matters differently in each category. Hand-tuning the weights does not scale beyond a few signals.
steps.fix: Take the top 300 candidates and score them with a learned ranking model, usually gradient-boosted trees trained with a ranking loss, or a small neural network. Its inputs are features about the query (category, length), the product (price, rating, stock, age), their match (BM25 per field, how many query words appear, price against the typical price for the category) and recent behaviour (clicks and purchases over the last hour and day). Features come from a feature store with a batch layer for slow ones and a streaming layer for fresh counts, fetched for all 300 candidates in one batched call. The stage has a deadline of about 30 ms: if it is missed, or the store is slow, the cheap first-stage order is returned.
steps.tradeoff: The learned model uses signals no hand-tuned formula can balance, and moves business metrics more than any other stage. The cost is a model to train and serve, a feature store that is now on the critical path, and a latency budget that caps the number of candidates and the model size.

steps.title: Log what was shown, with its position, to learn from it
steps.problem: The model needs labels, and the clicks are the cheapest ones. But shoppers click the first results far more than the same product lower down, so a click says as much about the position as about the product. Training on raw clicks teaches the model to reproduce the old ranking.
steps.fix: Log every impression: the query, the model version, each product shown and its position, plus the clicks, add-to-carts and purchases that follow, joined by a search id. Events go through a durable log with unique ids so duplicates can be dropped. Training reads this log and corrects for position bias: either each click is weighted by the inverse of the chance that its position was looked at (inverse propensity weighting, with the propensities estimated from small randomised swaps of neighbouring positions), or the position is a feature during training and fixed to one value when serving. Purchases count more than clicks, and clicks followed by a quick return to the results count less.
steps.tradeoff: The training data comes from real behaviour at the scale of billions of impressions a month. It is still observational: shoppers can only click what they were shown, and weighting by inverse propensity lowers the bias but raises the variance, so rarely seen positions need clipping.

steps.title: Measure every change offline first, then online
steps.problem: A new model can look better on the training metric and worse for shoppers. Without a trusted measurement, every release is a guess, and the metric that moves in the lab may not be the one that matters in the shop.
steps.fix: Offline: a set of a few thousand judged queries, where raters grade the results of sampled queries from 0 to 3 (the grade is kept with the product). A ranking is scored with NDCG@10, which gives more credit for high grades and discounts lower positions by log2(position + 1). The set is stratified so that rare queries are counted as well as head ones, and refreshed from time to time. A change that does not win offline never ships. Online: the survivors get an A/B test in which the search id is hashed to a bucket. The main metric is a business one (purchases per search, revenue per search) with guardrails: latency, zero-result rate, and the share of new products shown. Most gains are small, so a test runs long enough for a stable result, and the new model starts at 1% of traffic.
steps.tradeoff: Offline metrics are cheap and quick, and screen many ideas a day. They are biased by what the old system showed, and they are not the same as sales, so the A/B test decides. A/B tests are slow and use real shoppers, so only the best candidates get one.

steps.title: Give new products a chance and break the feedback loop
steps.problem: Products that were shown get clicks, so they are shown more, while products that were never shown cannot get the clicks that would earn them a place. A new product has no history, so the model scores it low, and the loop narrows the catalogue to the already popular.
steps.fix: Cold start gets its own treatment. A new product receives content-based features (category, price, text and image embeddings) and a prior from its category's average, so it is not scored as zero. An exploration slot reserves one position on a small share of searches for a product with few impressions, chosen with a bandit rule such as Thompson sampling, so every product gets a minimum number of impressions and the data is not only about the current winners. These impressions are logged as exploration, so training knows what was chosen at random. Guardrails in every A/B test check catalogue coverage and the share of impressions on new products, and part of the training data comes from less personalised, less popular-biased lists.
steps.tradeoff: The ranking keeps learning about the whole catalogue and sellers see a fair start. Exploration has a visible cost, since a slot goes to a product that is probably worse than the best known one, so the rate is small (a few percent) and capped per query.

failures.scenario: The feature store is slow or down
failures.impact: Every search waits for the re-ranker's features, and the p99 goes over 150 ms for everybody, or the search returns errors.
failures.answer: The feature call has its own deadline (about 15 ms), and a circuit breaker opens when it fails often. Missing features are replaced by category defaults, and when the whole re-ranker is skipped the first-stage order is returned, marked as degraded in the logs. A local cache of the most popular products' features absorbs short outages, so one dependency costs quality, not availability.

failures.scenario: A new model scores well offline but conversion drops in production
failures.impact: Revenue per search falls a little, which is hard to see by eye, and thousands of shoppers are served a worse order every minute.
failures.answer: The model is released through a feature flag at 1% of traffic with automatic guardrails on latency, zero-result rate and purchases per search. Each impression records the model version, so the result is explained by bucket. A rollback is a flag change. Afterwards the team looks for the gap: features computed differently in training and serving (skew), or judged queries that do not look like real traffic.

failures.scenario: The feedback loop narrows the catalogue
failures.impact: The same few hundred products fill the first pages, new products get no impressions, and sellers leave.
failures.answer: Impressions are logged with their positions, training corrects for position, and an exploration slot gives low-exposure products a minimum number of impressions. Every A/B test has a guardrail on catalogue coverage and on the share of impressions that go to products younger than 30 days. A periodic randomised slice of traffic measures what shoppers do when the model did not choose.

failures.scenario: Click data is stale, missing or duplicated
failures.impact: Features such as recent sales stop updating, or events are counted twice, so the model ranks on a distorted picture of what is popular.
failures.answer: Events carry a unique id and the pipeline de-duplicates on it. Counts of events per hour are monitored against the same hour last week, and the lag of the streaming layer is alerted on. Features carry their computation time, and the ranker treats anything older than its limit as missing instead of trusting it. A rebuild from the durable log repairs the counters.

failures.scenario: A traffic spike makes the re-ranker the slowest part
failures.impact: Queueing in the ranker fleet adds latency to every search, and the p99 passes the budget although each request is cheap.
failures.answer: The ranker fleet autoscales on queue length, and each request carries a deadline: if there is not enough time left when it reaches the ranker, it skips re-ranking. Under heavy load the number of candidates is cut from 300 to 100, and low-value traffic (bots, deep pages) is shed first.

alternatives.title: What the second stage optimises

options.name: Hand-tuned weights on a few signals
options.pro: Simple, explainable and fast to change
options.con: Cannot balance dozens of signals, and every tuning is an argument

options.name: A learned model (trees or a small network)
options.pro: Uses many features and fits to real behaviour
options.con: Needs labels, a feature store and an evaluation process

options.name: A large cross-encoder model on every pair
options.pro: Understands the meaning of the query against the text
options.con: Milliseconds per pair, so only the top 20 to 50 candidates fit in the budget

alternatives.pick: A learned tree model on 300 candidates is the default. A heavy neural model can reorder a short final list if its gain pays for the cost.

alternatives.title: What counts as a label

options.name: Raw clicks
options.con: Biased by position and by titles that attract clicks

options.name: Purchases and add-to-carts
options.pro: Closer to the shopper's real goal
options.con: Rarer, delayed, and zero for a shopper who bought elsewhere

options.name: Human judgments
options.pro: Unbiased by the old ranking, and good for evaluation
options.con: Expensive, so only thousands of queries

alternatives.pick: Train on position-corrected purchases and clicks, and keep human judgments for evaluation and for catching what the behaviour data cannot.

alternatives.title: How to judge a ranking change

options.name: Offline NDCG on judged queries
options.con: Not the same as sales, and judged queries can drift from real ones

options.name: Interleaving two rankings in one result list
options.pro: Needs far less traffic than a split test to find a preference
options.con: Shows a preference, not the size of the business effect

options.name: A/B test on a business metric
options.pro: Measures what matters, including long-term effects
options.con: Slow, and every test puts real shoppers at risk

alternatives.pick: Screen with NDCG, optionally confirm the direction by interleaving, and decide with an A/B test and guardrails.

alternatives.title: How fresh the features are

options.name: Daily batch features
options.pro: Cheap and simple, and the same in training and serving
options.con: A product that sells out or goes viral is ranked on yesterday's picture

options.name: Streaming counters in the feature store
options.pro: Minutes-old signals for popularity, stock and price
options.con: A streaming job to run, and training must see the same values

options.name: Compute the features at query time
options.con: No time for it in 150 ms, and it multiplies the load on every source

alternatives.pick: Batch for slow features, streaming for the few that change quickly, and logged feature values so training sees what serving saw.

quiz.question: A store trains its re-ranker on click logs from the current ranking. After launch, the new model keeps the old products in the top three slots, and an A/B test shows almost no gain. Shoppers click position 1 about five times as often as position 5, even for equally good products. What is the most effective fix for the training data?
options: Replace clicks with add-to-cart events as the only label, because adding to a cart is never affected by where a product appeared in the list
Add more title and brand features so the model can explain why products in the top slots were clicked
Weight each click by the inverse of the chance its position was looked at, estimated from small random swaps of neighbours
Train on the last 90 days of logs instead of 30, so a larger sample averages out the effect of position on the clicks, with no other change
quiz.explanation: Clicks mostly say where a product was shown, so the model learns the old order. Inverse propensity weighting, with propensities from small swaps, removes that effect. Add-to-carts and longer windows still come from the same biased list, and extra features cannot undo the label bias.

quiz.question: Your search has a 150 ms budget. Query understanding, retrieval with first-stage scoring, the feature fetch and result assembly use 95 ms together. The re-ranker scores one candidate in 250 microseconds of CPU and spreads one search over 4 threads. You want to keep 30% of the remaining time free for slow requests. About how many candidates can the re-ranker take?
options: About 880 candidates: all 55 ms that remain, times 4 threads, divided by 250 microseconds per candidate
About 150 candidates: 55 ms left, keep 70% of it, divided by 250 microseconds, with the 4 threads left out
About 220 candidates: all 55 ms that remain, divided by 250 microseconds, with the 4 threads left out
About 600: 55 ms left, keep 70%, times 4 threads, divided by 250 microseconds
quiz.explanation: 55 ms times 0.7 is 38.5 ms of wall time, which gives 154 ms of CPU on 4 threads, and 154,000 microseconds divided by 250 is about 616. Using all 55 ms ignores the safety margin and breaks the budget on slow requests, and leaving out the threads undercounts the capacity.

quiz.question: A new product from a small seller has excellent reviews elsewhere, but after three weeks it has had 12 impressions and no sales, and the model scores it low. The team already corrects clicks for position. Which change lets the system find out how good new products really are?
options: Reserve one slot on a few percent of searches for a product with few impressions, and log those as exploration
Multiply the final score of every product by 1.5 during its first 30 days, whatever its quality or its reviews, so that it climbs the list
Retrain the ranker every day instead of every week, so the model sees new sales sooner
Fix the ranking features for new products to the average of their category and stop updating them
quiz.explanation: The product is stuck because it is never shown, so there is no data to learn from, and position correction cannot create impressions. A small exploration slot gives it a minimum number of views and marks them as chosen on purpose. Retraining faster still has no data, and a blanket boost promotes weak new products as well as good ones.
